claims.text: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi has high saturation magnetization and a baseline coercivity of approximately 100 Oe.
Aging single-phase fcc FeCoNi at 600–700 °C for 3–6 hours can induce nanoscale BCC precipitates in the fcc matrix.
Rapid quenching after aging will retain the nanoscale BCC precipitates.
The aging treatment will produce coherent, uniformly dispersed, nanometer-scale BCC precipitates.
Nanoscale BCC precipitates will act as domain-wall pinning centers in FeCoNi.
Pinning by the precipitates will hinder domain-wall movement during magnetization reversal.
Hindering domain-wall motion will increase coercivity.
Aging time and temperature can be used to control precipitate size and volume fraction in FeCoNi.
Limiting precipitate size and volume fraction will prevent substantial dilution of the ferromagnetic matrix and preserve saturation magnetization.
The treatment will raise coercivity significantly above 100 Oe.
The treatment will leave saturation magnetization nearly unchanged.
The typical magnetic domain-wall thickness relevant to the proposed FeCoNi system is on the order of a few nanometers.
Precipitates well below the domain-wall thickness can nevertheless provide the proposed coercivity-enhancing pinning.
Conventional melting and casting will retain sufficient overall homogeneity for the proposed treatment.
The mechanism is applicable to bulk high-entropy or multi-principal-element alloys processed by melting and casting.
Coercivity, saturation magnetization, precipitate size, precipitate volume fraction, and phase identity can be measured using VSM, TEM, and XRD in treated and baseline samples.
The hypothesis is falsified if coercivity fails to increase by at least 20%, saturation magnetization decreases by more than 10%, or coherent nanoscale BCC precipitates are not observed.

contradictions.description: The conditions require precipitates well below the domain-wall thickness, while the mechanism requires those precipitates to pin domain walls. The cited evidence states that precipitates of a few nanometers below the domain-wall thickness do not interact with Bloch walls, so the specified size boundary undermines the proposed pinning mechanism.
